title: Jev classifies a tick's kind of work; config maps work to model
description:
Jev classifies the KIND OF WORK a tick is; the orchestrator's config maps a kind of work to a model.

THE SHAPE, and why it is this way round (operator, 2026-09-22). Jev is not asked which
model to use. It is asked what the work IS - a closed enum of work types - and the config
decides what that is worth. Each decision sits with whoever can make it: the classifier
judges the tick, the operator's table judges the cost.

That separation buys four things:
  - Changing model policy does not invalidate a recorded classification. Swap the model
    lineup, add a tier, change your mind about budget: you edit a table. "This is a docs
    tick" stays true; "this deserves flash" was only ever true against one lineup.
  - The recorded evidence means something to a person reading the run later. A work type
    explains why a run went the way it did; a tier name does not.
  - It matches the config shape that already exists. [roles.*.tiers.<name>] already maps a
    name to a model overlay; a work type is another key into that kind of table.
  - It is a better task for Jev. A closed enum is its sweet spot; weighing cost against
    capability is policy, not classification.

It also dissolves the promotion question below. "Nothing starts high on a DESCRIPTION"
guarded against prose buying an expensive model. A classified work type is not prose - it
is a fact, and the table decides what it costs - so promotion stops being a special case.

WHY, and what it changes. Today a first attempt's tier comes from [[tier_policy.start]] rules matching STRUCTURAL FACTS - type, role, priority, wave, how many ticks it blocks. Those are proxies for complexity, not judgements of it, and `max_blocks = 0` ("the mark of a mechanical tick") is about as close as a fact gets. A deterministic orchestrator cannot read a tick and decide whether the work is hard.

Operator, 2026-09-22: it should be able to ask. Jev (TypeSafe AI, early access 15 Sept 2026) is a "System One" model - text in, TYPED probabilistic decisions out, with confidence, in one parallel pass. About $0.042 per million input tokens with free output, 40-200x faster than a frontier model.

Three properties that make it the right instrument rather than just a cheap one:
  - It cannot produce a type error. The tier vocabulary is a closed enum (isKnownTier refuses anything else); a text model can answer "medium-high" and needs validating, Jev structurally cannot.
  - It returns CONFIDENCE. Low confidence is a third answer, not a coin flip - fall back to the policy's default, the same way run.cost_source distinguishes a zero from an unknown.
  - The cost is a rounding error, so "do not pay a model to decide what to pay a model" stops being an objection.

THE DECISION THAT OVERRIDES AN EXISTING RULE, stated so nobody later reads it as a bug.

internal/runconfig/tierpolicy.go says, and load.go enforces:

    "The one rule that makes the ladder a ladder rather than a wish: facts may
     make a first attempt CHEAPER, never dearer."
    "nothing starts high on a description - expense is earned by a failed
     attempt, not asserted by a rule"

Operator, 2026-09-22: "i think it should be allowed to go dearer."

That rule exists to stop a DESCRIPTION buying an expensive model - an author, or a model reading prose, talking its way up the ladder. The reason it is being relaxed is that Jev is not a description: it is a classifier with a confidence score, on a closed enum, priced so low that a wrong cheap guess costs more in wasted attempts than every classification in the epic costs to make. Starting a genuinely complex tick on flash so it can fail and climb is the waste the operator objected to, and it is real: a failed attempt is a model's full run, a wall clock, and a gate.

So promotion is allowed, BOUNDED BY THE CEILING. What is NOT relaxed:
  - The ceiling still bounds everything. At the ceiling the next actor is a person, not a bigger model.
  - Failure still escalates underneath. Jev picks a START; a failed attempt still earns a rung.
  - A tick's own prose still cannot promote it. The classifier may, an assertion in a description may not.

SHAPE
  1. First dispatch of a tick: the orchestrator asks Jev which WORK TYPE the tick is, from
     a closed enum declared in config, plus confidence. It is never asked for a model or a
     tier.
  2. The answer is written to the run branch as a decision record, like the review and closeout exchanges already are - "so a restart re-reads them instead of re-asking a model it already paid". This is axiom 1, not thrift: a re-derivation must reach the same dispatch, and a recorded classification does while a re-ask only probably does.
  3. Later passes, including after a restart, READ the record. Jev is asked once per tick.
  4. Low confidence, no answer, or Jev unavailable: fall back to [[tier_policy.start]] and the default. The feature degrades to today's behaviour rather than stopping a run.
  5. The config maps work type -> model, beside the existing [roles.*.tiers.*] overlays.
     A work type with no mapping falls back to the default, and says so, rather than
     failing a dispatch on a table someone forgot to extend.
  6. The recorded work type is an input to the policy, not a replacement for it: the
     ceiling, the step and the failure ladder all still apply on top.

OPEN, and worth settling before building:
  - Jev is in LIMITED EARLY ACCESS. Confirm access and terms before this becomes load-bearing, and keep (4) so the factory works without it.
  - What exactly is Jev shown? The tick's title, description and acceptance criteria are the obvious input; whether it also sees the repository's own conventions is a real question, because a tick that is trivial in one codebase is not in another.
  - What confidence threshold counts as "low"? Pick it from measurement, not taste - classify a set of already-run ticks and compare against how they actually went.
  - The work-type enum is PROPOSED BELOW and no longer open. What remains open about it
     is whether `construction` sits on the right side of the flash/full line, which the
     measurement below is the way to settle.
  - Two models today (GLM 5.3 Flash, GLM 5.3), so several work types will map to the same
     model. That is fine and is the point: the enum describes the work, the table describes
     what it costs, and they are allowed to be different shapes.

THE WORK-TYPE ENUM (operator asked for a proposal, 2026-09-22; this is it)

The axis is INFERENCE UNDER UNCERTAINTY - how much of the work is deciding what to do
rather than doing it. Size and risk were considered and rejected: a large mechanical edit
is still mechanical, and a risky one-line change is still one line. What separated flash
from full in this week's actual runs was how much had to be worked out.

  mechanical    the change is stated, not decided. Done is knowable by construction.
  translation   a known pattern applied to new material. Done is knowable by comparison.
  construction  build to a stated spec; decisions are local. Done is the acceptance.
  diagnosis     cause unknown. Form and discard hypotheses against evidence. Done is
                knowable only once the cause is found.
  design        the shape itself is in question, and the tick's own framing may be wrong.
                Done is knowable only by argument.

Ordered on purpose. Adding a third model later moves ONE boundary instead of
re-classifying anything, and the recorded classifications stay valid.

GROUNDED IN TICKS THIS REPOSITORY ACTUALLY RAN, which is the test of whether an enum is
real rather than plausible:

  mechanical    f8l - delete hello.txt and goodbye.txt. GLM did it in nine tool calls.
  translation   lk9 - add a guard test in the shape of the existing `serial:` guard.
  construction  8xd - a streaming tar reader to a stated spec.
                prs - put the ticfac binaries in the orchestrator image.
  diagnosis     qsn - a detached `git maintenance` child corrupting the NEXT test's
                fixture; found with GIT_TRACE2_EVENT after two wrong hypotheses.
                m78 - the tracker and the gate both naming their worktree `tree`.
  design        yoh - where the orchestrator runs.
                wne - this ticket.

MAPPING, with two models today:

    mechanical, translation, construction  -> glm-5.3-flash
    diagnosis, design                      -> glm-5.3

`construction` is deliberately the contentious one. It is the boundary case, and it is
where the failure ladder earns its keep rather than where classification has to be right.

WHY THIS IS NOT ticks' `type` FIELD. `task`/`bug`/`epic` describes the TICKET - who filed
it and what it is about. This describes the WORK. A bug can be mechanical (a typo with a
known fix) or diagnosis (an intermittent failure with no repro), and those two want
different models. Keeping them separate is the whole point.

JEV IS FALLIBLE, AND THE LADDER ALREADY HANDLES IT (operator, 2026-09-22: "a tick that
fails on a low model may need to get mechanically upgraded to a larger").

That is the existing mechanism, unchanged: Jev picks the START, each FAILED attempt earns
a rung upward, bounded by the ceiling, and at the ceiling the next actor is a person.
A mis-classified `construction` tick fails on flash and becomes full with nobody in the
loop. Classification makes the FIRST attempt smarter; escalation makes a wrong
classification cheap. Neither has to be perfect for the pair to be good.

MEASURE BEFORE TRUSTING IT. Classify ~20 already-run ticks from Phase 4 and Phase 5 and
compare the predicted tier against how they actually went - the attempt history, the
failures, the escalations are all on the run branches. That is the only honest way to pick
the confidence threshold, and it is cheap: the ticks exist and Jev costs $0.042 per
million input tokens. Do this before the classifier is load-bearing, not after.
acceptance_criteria: A tick is classified once into the five work types, the classification is recorded on the run branch and re-read on restart, the config maps each work type to a model, a failed attempt still climbs a rung, and an unclassifiable tick or an absent Jev falls back to tier_policy rather than stopping the run
